Scientific name
Habit
Leaf and twig
Flowers
Fruits
Small-leaved lime
Tilia cordata
Tilleul à petites feuilles
Heart-shaped leaves with an asymmetric base; small rusty hair tufts below vein junctions. Flowers and fruits are attached to a long pale bract.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Rowan
Sorbus aucuparia
Sorbier des oiseleurs
Alternate leaves, usually with 9–15 toothed leaflets. White flowers in dense clusters. Small orange-red pomes, not true botanical berries.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Blackthorn
Prunus spinosa
Prunellier
Shrub with many thorny twigs. Small toothed leaves. White flowers often precede the leaves; blue-black sloes have a pale waxy bloom.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common elder
Sambucus nigra
Sureau noir
Opposite leaves with 5–7 toothed leaflets. Broad flat clusters of tiny cream flowers. Black fruits in drooping clusters when ripe; twigs have white pith.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Guelder rose
Viburnum opulus
Viorne obier
Opposite three-lobed leaves. Large sterile flowers surround small fertile central flowers. Translucent red fruits; the wild form differs from snowball cultivars.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Common gorse
Ulex europaeus
Ajonc d’Europe
Dense shrub with many spiny shoots and spine-like leaves. Yellow flowers with a hairy calyx; short hairy pods. Flowering may extend well beyond the main season.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Sweet violet
Viola odorata
Violette odorante
Heart-shaped leaves; flowers have five unequal petals and a rear spur. A creeping, stolon-forming plant, usually with scented flowers. Other violets require examination of stipules and hairs.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Red clover
Trifolium pratense
Trèfle des prés
Three oval leaflets, often with a pale chevron. Upright hairy stems. Pink to purple pea flowers form dense heads close to the upper leaves.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
White clover
Trifolium repens
Trèfle blanc
Creeping stems root at the nodes. Three rounded leaflets, often pale-marked. White flower heads on long stalks; older flowers bend downwards.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Tufted vetch
Vicia cracca
Vesce cracca
Leaves have many narrow leaflets and end in a branched tendril. Climbs through surrounding vegetation. Long one-sided racemes of violet flowers; flattened pods.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Stinging nettle
Urtica dioica
Grande ortie
Opposite coarsely toothed leaves; stems and leaves bear stinging hairs. Tiny greenish flowers in axillary clusters; male and female flowers usually on separate plants.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Meadow sage
Salvia pratensis
Sauge des prés
Large wrinkled basal leaves and opposite stem leaves. Blue-violet flowers have an arched upper lip and form spaced tiers; two fertile stamens.
Found in mainland France; frequency and local occurrence vary.
Tilia platyphyllos
Large-leaved lime
Tilleul à larges feuilles; large leaved linden
Large heart-shaped leaves are hairy beneath, with pale hair tufts at vein junctions. Hanging flowers share an elongated bract. The small, hard fruits have five prominent ribs.
Ravine woods, cool slopes and mountains; also planted in parks and villages.
Salix alba
White willow
Saule argenté; silver willow
Long, finely toothed lanceolate leaves have silky hairs, especially beneath. Catkins appear with the leaves. Male and female trees are separate; capsules release seeds with long hairs.
Riverbanks, ditches and floodplains across much of France.
Ulmus minor
Field elm
Ormeau; smooth-leaved elm

Short-stalked leaves have strongly unequal bases and double teeth. Small flowers without petals appear before the leaves. Rounded samaras are notched at the tip, with the seed near the notch; suckering is frequent.
Hedges, woods and valleys; often survives as young suckers where Dutch elm disease has removed mature trees.
Viburnum lantana
Wayfaring tree
Mancienne; viorne mancienne; wayfaring tree
Opposite, thick, wrinkled oval leaves are felted beneath. All the small flowers in the cluster are fertile. Drupes turn from green to red and then black, often at different stages within one cluster.
Rather dry hedges and woodland edges, especially on limestone.
Salix caprea
Goat willow
Marsault; saule des chèvres; pussy willow
A large shrub or small tree with broad, wrinkled leaves, felted beneath. Oval male catkins turn from silver to yellow before the leaves emerge. Female plants later bear capsules with silky seeds.
Woodland edges, clearings and fresh soils; tolerates drier ground than many willows.
Vaccinium myrtillus
Bilberry
Brimbelle; airelle myrtille; European blueberry

A small deciduous shrub with angular green stems. Leaves are finely toothed; solitary urn-shaped flowers are pinkish to greenish. Bloom-coated blue-black berries have coloured flesh, unlike many large cultivated blueberries.
Acidic woodland, heaths and mountains; scarce on lowland limestone.
Silene dioica
Red campion
Silène dioïque; Lychnis dioica; red campion

A hairy plant with opposite leaves. Five deeply notched pink petals emerge from a fused calyx; male and female flowers are on separate plants. The plate shows a female flower with five styles. Capsules open by ten rolled-back teeth.
Cool woodland edges, hedges and damp woods; scarcer in the dry south.
Rabelera holostea
Greater stitchwort
Stellaria holostea; langue d’oiseau; greater stitchwort

Narrow, opposite, stalkless leaves have rough margins. Each flower has five white petals split about halfway, rather than ten petals. Capsules have six teeth. Many floras still use the name Stellaria holostea.
Hedges, shady banks and woodland edges, often forming springtime patches.
Veronica chamaedrys
Germander speedwell
Fausse germandrée; germander speedwell

Opposite toothed leaves and two lines of hairs on the stem. Lateral racemes bear blue flowers with white throats. The corolla has four unequal lobes and two stamens; capsules are flattened and heart-shaped.
Meadows, hedges, banks and open woods; common across much of France.
Umbrella thorn
Acacia tortilis · acacia raddiana

A spreading crown often forms an umbrella. Tiny leaflets are carried on paired pinnae. Long straight thorns and short hooked thorns may coexist. Cream flower heads give way to narrow, coiled, usually indehiscent pods.
Dry African savannas and semi-desert regions, from northern and Sahelian areas to eastern and southern Africa; forms vary by subspecies.
Tamarind
Tamarin · tamarind

Dense rounded crown and leaves with many paired oblong leaflets, without a terminal leaflet or tendril. Three conspicuous yellow petals carry red veins; two other petals are reduced. Brown brittle pods remain closed around pulp and hard seeds.
Native to tropical Africa and widely cultivated throughout the tropics. African savannas, wooded sites and villages.
Senegal senna
Cassia italica · Cassia obovata · séné d’Italie

Low perennial or subshrub with paired, blunt leaflets and no terminal tendril. Yellow flowers have five unequal petals and conspicuous unequal anthers. The flattened pods are curved. Habit and hairiness vary among subspecies.
Dry sandy or stony habitats across much of Africa, including the Sahel; its native range extends to the Indian subcontinent.
Indian jujube
Jujube · ber · Ziziphus mauritiana

Thorny shrub or tree with drooping branches. The shiny leaves show three strong veins from the base and a pale hairy underside. Tiny greenish flowers grow in axillary clusters. Wild drupes are smaller than those of many cultivated forms.
Widespread in warm African drylands and cultivated near settlements; also widespread in Asia. It may grow as a tree where conditions permit.
Winged-seed sesame
Sésame de gazelle · Sesamopteris alata

Annual with generally opposite leaves, rarely alternate, strongly differing along the stem: lower leaves are deeply divided or have three to five narrow leaflets; upper leaves are simple. Pink tubular flowers have darker lines on the lower lip. Beaked capsules contain seeds winged at both ends.
Widespread in tropical Africa south to Namibia and South Africa; sandy roadsides, grasslands and seasonal river beds.
Vachellia tortilis
Tamarindus indica
Senna italica
Ziziphus mauritiana
Sesamum alatum
Giant sequoia
Giant redwood; Wellingtonia; séquoia de Wellington

A huge, long-lived conifer with a broad, buttressed trunk and reddish fibrous bark. Short pointed leaves overlap around cord-like shoots. Ovoid cones have thick shield-like scales. Old crowns become rounded and irregular.
Native to scattered groves on the western slopes of the Sierra Nevada, California. Planted in parks on other continents.
Sequoiadendron giganteum
Coast redwood
Coastal redwood; séquoia à feuilles d’if

A towering evergreen with a long straight trunk. Shaded lateral shoots carry flattened leaves in two apparent ranks, with pale stomatal bands beneath; exposed shoots also bear short scale-like leaves. Small woody cones have shield-like scales.
Native to the fog-influenced Pacific coast of northern and central California and southwestern Oregon.
Sequoia sempervirens
Highbush blueberry
Blueberry; bleuet en corymbe; bleuet américain

Upright deciduous shrub of acidic ground. Clusters of small urn-shaped flowers precede blue berries with a waxy bloom and a persistent calyx crown. It is a major parent of cultivated highbush blueberries.
Eastern North America, in moist woods, swamps and acidic clearings. Cultivated widely outside its native range.
Vaccinium corymbosum
Bread wheat
Triticum aestivum
Common wheat · Blé tendre · Froment

Annual cereal producing several tillers from the base. Jointed culms have mostly hollow internodes; alternate leaves have a sheath, a flat blade, a short membranous ligule and clasping auricles, often hairy. The terminal spike carries sessile spikelets on opposite sides of its axis. Each spikelet has several florets enclosed by glumes, lemmas and paleas. A fertile floret has three stamens and two feathery stigmas. Each grain is a caryopsis with a longitudinal ventral crease. Awn length varies greatly; the drawing represents a short-awned form.

Domesticated hexaploid wheat, widely cultivated in temperate regions and suitable uplands. Winter and spring forms differ in their seasonal requirements. Cultivation, soil conditions and cultivar strongly influence height and ear shape.
Several jointed tillers, narrow sheathing leaves and upright terminal spikes.
Parallel-veined blade; enlarged junction on the right shows the sheath, short ligule and clasping hairy auricles.
Main spike: alternating sessile spikelets with several florets. Enlarged open floret on the right: three stamens and two feathery stigmas.
Enlarged naked caryopsis with a ventral crease and an apical brush of hairs; a mature spike is shown at a smaller scale.
Maize
Zea mays
Corn · Maïs

Tall annual grass with a stout, pith-filled culm and broad alternate leaves arranged in two ranks. Each leaf has a clasping sheath, a short ligule and a prominent midrib. Male flowers form the terminal tassel; female flowers occupy separate ears in the leaf axils on the same plant. The silks are elongated styles and stigmas that receive airborne pollen. The mature ear bears rows of caryopses on a cob, surrounded by leafy husks. Grain colour, ear size and plant height vary greatly among cultivars.

Crop domesticated in Mexico and now cultivated worldwide where seasonal warmth permits. The plate shows a conventional grain-maize form; it does not represent the full diversity of maize landraces or wild teosintes.
Thick jointed culm, broad leaves in two ranks, terminal male tassel, axillary female ear and basal brace roots.
Broad blade with a pale midrib and parallel veins; inset shows its sheathing base and short membranous ligule.
Left: branched male tassel with hanging anthers. Right: female ear inside leafy husks, with a tuft of silks; these are not stamens.
Main subject: mature ear with rows of grains and peeled-back husks. Right: enlarged individual caryopsis with its embryo region indicated.
Potato
Solanum tuberosum
Pomme de terre · Irish potato

Tuber-forming perennial usually grown as an annual crop. The aerial stems carry alternate compound leaves with large oval leaflets and smaller intercalary ones. White to violet flowers have a broad, fused, five-lobed corolla and yellow anthers opening by terminal pores. Some plants develop small greenish berries containing seeds; these berries are not edible. Underground stolons swell into tubers whose eyes are buds: the tuber is a stem organ, distinct from the fruit and from a root.

Domesticated South American crop, now cultivated worldwide in suitable climates. Tuber formation, flowering and fruit set depend strongly on the variety and growing conditions. Vegetative propagation through tubers does not make the tuber a seed.
Leafy aerial stems above a schematic soil line; below, lateral stolons end in tubers. Roots are omitted to keep these stem organs clear.
Compound leaf with broad principal leaflets and smaller intercalary ones; margins are much less deeply cut than in the tomato example.
Broad violet corolla with five fused lobes; five yellow anthers with terminal pores surround the style. White-flowered varieties also occur.
Large green sphere: the seed-bearing berry, not edible. Separate brown inset: a stolon tuber with bud eyes, drawn at an independent scale.
Common thyme
Thymus vulgaris
Common thyme Thymus vulgaris
Small aromatic subshrub with a woody base. Leaf edges are often rolled under.
Southern Europe; widely cultivated.
Short shoots arising from a woody base.
Small opposite narrow leaves with entire margins.
Two-lipped pink to white corolla.
Four nutlets within the persistent calyx, enlarged.
Rye
Secale cereale
Rye Secale cereale
Annual cereal, distinct from Lolium ryegrasses. Spikelets usually contain two fertile florets.
Domesticated in Turkey; cultivated worldwide.
Upright culms and narrow spike.
Linear blade, sheath and small auricles.
Spikelets along the rachis; awns and enlarged floret.
Elongated caryopsis; mature spike in the inset.
Fenugreek
Trigonella foenum-graecum
Fenugreek Trigonella foenum-graecum
Aromatic annual cultivated for leaves and seeds. Its pods are long and narrow.
Southeastern Europe and western Asia; cultivated elsewhere.
Upright branched stems with alternate leaves.
Three leaflets, toothed mainly towards their tips.
Pale pea-shaped flowers in leaf axils.
Slender opened pod containing numerous seeds.
White mustard
Sinapis alba
White mustard Sinapis alba
Often bristly annual. “White” names the mustard, not its flower colour.
Europe, North Africa and western Asia; introduced elsewhere.
Branched stem and divided foliage.
Lobed leaf with a large terminal lobe.
Four yellow petals arranged in a cross.
Hairy silique with flattened beak; opened valves reveal a few seeds.
Ginger
Zingiber officinale
Zingiber officinale

Harvested ginger is a branched rhizome: an underground stem with buds and roots, not a fruit or a true root. Leafy shoots and separate leafless flower spikes arise from it. Each asymmetric flower has one fertile stamen and a coloured lip derived from sterile stamens. Flowering and fruiting are uncommon in cultivation.
Cultivated in tropical regions, with Asian origins; reproduction depends on growing conditions.
Leafy shoots and separate bracted spike above a branched rhizome.
Narrow alternate blades in two ranks, with parallel veins.
Bracted spike and enlarged asymmetric flower: coloured lip and one fertile stamen.
Rare three-valved capsule; the rhizome inset is a stem, not a fruit.
Lingonberry
Vaccinium vitis-idaea
Vaccinium vitis-idaea

A low evergreen ericaceous shrub with leathery leaves and red berries. Short racemes bear fused bell-shaped corollas, usually four-lobed, with eight stamens. Rhizomes form spreading patches. Leaf persistence and red fruits distinguish it from deciduous bilberry.
Northern temperate and boreal regions of the Northern Hemisphere, especially woods and heaths.
Low woody shoots in an evergreen patch.
Small leathery oval leaf with rounded tip.
Four-lobed bell and enlarged end view with eight stamens.
Red berries in a short terminal raceme.
Creeping willow
Salix repens
Salix repens

A low deciduous willow spreading through creeping stems. Small leaves often have a silky silver underside. Male and female catkins occur on separate plants, without petals. Female flowers form two-valved capsules releasing hairy seeds. Habit and hairiness vary strongly.
Europe, especially wet heaths and dunes; some forms are much taller than the low habit illustrated.
Creeping woody axes with short upright leafy shoots.
Small oval leaf with silvery marginal hairs.
Male catkin with paired stamens; female catkin enlarged separately.
Two-valved capsule and seeds with a tuft of fine hairs.
Soapwort
Saponaria officinalis
Saponaria officinalis

A spreading rhizomatous perennial with opposite leaves and conspicuous longitudinal veins. Wild-type flowers have five pale petals, ten stamens and two styles; double garden forms differ. The persistent tubular calyx surrounds a dry capsule opening by four apical teeth.
Eurasia; cultivated and naturalized in many temperate regions.
Branching leafy stems arising from spreading underground axes.
Opposite blade with three strong basal longitudinal veins.
Five pale petals, ten stamens and two styles.
Four-toothed dry capsule; the calyx remains around its base.
White campion
Silene latifolia
Silene latifolia

A usually dioecious campion with opposite hairy leaves: male and female flowers grow on separate plants. The five white petals are deeply split. Female flowers have five styles and an enlarged ribbed calyx; their capsules commonly show ten teeth as five valves divide again.
Native to Europe and introduced widely, including North America.
Opposite leafy stems and branching white flowers.
Opposite oval blade with fine hairs.
Female flower with five split petals, five styles and inflated calyx inset.
Ten-toothed capsule within its persistent ribbed calyx.
Coltsfoot
Tussilago farfara
Tussilago farfara

A rhizomatous perennial whose scaly flower stalks usually appear before the broad foliage leaves. Yellow heads contain many narrow peripheral ray florets and central disc florets. Later leaves have a woolly underside. Fruits carry a pappus of fine hairs; flowering and leafy stages are shown separately.
Europe, northern Africa and northern/western Asia; introduced elsewhere. Seasons differ between hemispheres.
Leafless scaly flowering stalk; later leafy stage in a separate inset.
Broad heart-based leaf with shallow teeth and hairy underside.
Yellow flower head: many ray florets surrounding disc florets.
Slender one-seeded fruit with a long fine-haired pappus.
Swedish whitebeam
Sorbus intermedia Scandosorbus intermedia
Sorbus intermedia

A deciduous whitebeam with simple lobed leaves, unlike the pinnate leaves of rowan. The pale felted underside contrasts with the dark upper face. White flowers form corymbs and mature into orange-red pomes. Its hybrid and polyploid history is more complex than one bifurcation in a teaching tree.
Northern European origins; also planted in temperate urban and coastal landscapes. The archive retains the name Sorbus intermedia.
Broad-crowned deciduous tree.
One simple toothed and lobed blade; a pale underside is shown separately.
White five-petalled flowers in a corymb.
Orange-red pomes with persistent calyx remnants.
Common vetch
Vicia sativa
Vicia sativa

An annual climbing legume with pinnate leaves ending in tendrils. Leaflets often have a notched tip. Usually one or two purple pea flowers occur in a leaf axil. Each flower has one carpel, which forms an elongated pod containing several seeds.
Eurasian origins and a long history of cultivation; introduced in many regions.
Leafy climbing or sprawling shoot.
Paired leaflets and a terminal tendril; representative notched tips.
Pea flower with standard, wings and keel.
Elongated pod opening along two sutures to expose seeds.
Hedge vetch
Vicia sepium
Vicia sepium

A perennial climbing vetch with broad paired leaflets and terminal tendrils. Short axillary groups contain several purple flowers, unlike the usually solitary or paired flowers of common vetch. Leaflet number varies. Each flower matures into a several-seeded legume.
Europe and temperate Asia; introduced in North America and elsewhere.
Leafy scrambling perennial shoot.
Broad paired leaflets with a terminal tendril.
Short group of pea flowers on an axillary axis.
Several-seeded legume with two opening valves.
